"If they add too many features they will overcomplicated the game" is a dumb excuse for the minimal updates.

While 1.21 and 1.20 were, in my opinion, pretty good updates, I believe that they could be much better. And while I could talk about quality, in this post I will talk about quantity. And I'm not the only one who thinks that Minecraft updates are small and shallow, and that these updates should be bigger.
But one argument I often hear is "well the game would be too cluttered if the updates were bigger" "Mojang can do bigger updates, they just don't want to. They could make an impressive update that would significantly improve the game, but they don't, so enjoy the game as it is". And this argument is just so, so dumb imo. Obviously, having this opinion is valid, but I strongly disagree with you.
And for one main reason: the game is already pretty complicated. Minecraft in general is a pretty complicated game, full of features that most players probably won't explore them in their entirety, and that's
OK. The game itself has a lot of clutter anyway. Don't believe me? When was the last time you had a pet parrot or a pet fox? When was the last time you've interacted with the Sniffer? How many of you use diorite, granite, and andesite frequently in your builds? How many of you have even tried the new archeology mechanic?
I'm just tired of people shutting down any kind of request for more complex updates, by just saying that the game needs to be simple, and having bigger updates would be way too much. Buddy, the game hasn't been simple since like 2013. In the past decade, Minecraft has added a lot of "Clutter". The problem is that a lot of this clutter has been pretty much forgotten by the entire community. Not thay many people have crafted Spyglass and Crossbow yet, like ever.
Also the game is filled with the brim with mobs that pretty much don't do anything. So why doesn't Mojang add "Clutter" that's much beefier and much more ambitious? New Biomes like a Redwood and Wisteria Forest? New crops and plants. New mobs like butterflies and deers, that you can kill to get vineson. Maybe an oven or cooking pot that lets you cook meals that fill your hunger bar for longer periods of time.
"Well a beefy update like a good Farming or Nature Update is just too much man, it would overwhelm the players" no it won't. We've seen time and time again how updates like The Aquatic or The Village and Pillage update were welcome by the majority of people. If you can't handle more than 3 mobs and 2 blocks per update, that doesn't mean that we don't too.
If you find the game too complicated, go and play in an older version and let us have an update that's less shallow and adds enough stuff to satisfy most people.
And I ain't saying that the more recent updates are bad , but shallow, and lack depth, leaving for untapped potential. Why didn't the Sniffer.... sniff more plants? Maybe new crops? Maybe expand on the archeology mechanic by adding more items that you could find, new or already existent. This is not me crapping on Mojang, but giving my take. text:
Wish the game had more to it

Minecraft has so many systems that look like they should matter—combat, gear progression, stronger materials, structures, mobs—but none of them actually lead anywhere. Once you beat the Ender Dragon and Wither, there’s no real reason to keep engaging with survival mechanics because nothing pushes back anymore. Building ends up being the only meaningful activity, but even that lacks purpose because your base doesn’t need to defend you from anything.
Why have stronger blocks, traps, or better weapons if there’s no threat that requires them? I’m not asking for some grindy RPG system or constant attacks, just a reason for survival to still feel like survival later in the game. Give building a function, give mobs a purpose beyond early game, and give players something to do that isn’t just building for the sake of it.
I do understand this game is more geared towards building, but in my opinion there are three types of players: builders, redstone players, and fighters. Yet the game only ever really favours builders. Take the Creaking for example—it’s a cool mob with a unique mechanic, but the only real reason to go to that biome is for the wood. A lot of Minecraft just feels like one loop now: new biome, maybe a new mob that doesn’t really do much, and the only reason to go there is for the blocks.
It just feels like the game sets up all these systems—combat, gear, structures—but never actually gives them a proper purpose. I don’t think it needs to turn into some grindy RPG, but it would be nice if survival, combat, and exploration actually mattered as much as building does.

text:
Earmuffs for Allays - Keep them as useful companions without them bonding to nearby Note Blocks

The problem:
Allays currently link to any active note block nearby, even when the player doesn't want them to. For example, if you are using an Allay as a companion while gathering wood or mining, simply walking past your base's farms that include note blocks will cause the Allay to link to that note block and abandon you.

The solution: Wool Earmuffs
In Minecraft, wool already dampens sound vibrations (used against Sculk Sensors and the Warden). Allowing players to equip Allays with Wool Earmuffs would be a natural and consistent addition to the game's mechanics.

How It Would Work:

  * Crafting: Crafted simply with 2 Wool and 3 Iron Nuggets for the headband.

  * Equipping: Right-click an Allay to put them on. Sneak + right-click with an empty hand to take them back.
  * Effect: While wearing the earmuffs, the Allay can't hear note block vibrations. It will never link to note blocks and will strictly remain a faithful companion to the player, helping them build tall structures (by bringing back fallen blocks) and gather resources.

  * Visuals & Customization: They show up as tiny, adorable earmuffs on the Allay's head and can be crafted in all 16 wool colors!
I've also submitted this to the official Minecraft Feedback site if you'd like to support the idea there: https://feedback.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/community/posts/48978540335501-Earmuffs-for-Allays

The in-game visuals were custom-made by me using Blockbench and rendered in-game to show how this feature could look.

What are genuine arguments against an item stack increase?

According to the wiki, there are 1,643 items in the game as of 1.20 (the number is gonna be even higher after this next content drop).

lets compare this to terraria
In terraria, 1.2 increased the item stack limit from 250 to 999. Can't get a solid number, but there were about 1,800 items in terraria in 1.2. Terraria also increased the chest storage size from 30-40 in 1.2, had dedicated ammo and trash slots in 1.0.6, and quick stack, sorting, and deposit all buttons in 1.3.
Minecraft has almost the same amount of items as there were in terraria 1.2, but there has not been an item stack increase in the entire lifespan of the game, or even any kind of inventory management other than bundles and shulker boxes (shulker's are endgame content).
you can make the argument that they are different games with different needs, but if anything that points to Minecraft needing an item increase more than terraria does. Minecraft, as a 3d game, needs far more building materials than terraria. Minecraft has a smaller base inventory size than terraria (37 vs 50, not including dedicated ammo, money, and multiple armor and accessory slots), and has far fewer options for remote storage.
To have 250 items in Minecraft, you need to dedicate 4 inventory slots, which is 10% of your inventory. Pre 1.2 terraria, 250 items took up 2% of your inventory.
So what do you guys think? I feel like we're getting to the point where stack increases, and other inventory management, are becoming necessary. I dont wanna hear any BS about how 64 is an iconic number, that's just using nostalgia as an excuse to not move forward with the game. nothing will stop you from keeping your own stacks at 64 if you like the number

How do you want Minecraft to look in 10 years time?

I feel like this is the kind of discussion and feedback that would actually help Mojang get out of the cycle of lots of gimmicky incoherent and half-baked updates that don't really interact with each other. As a community we need to feed them big strategic long-term ideas, not just lots of little fixes or gimmicks here and there.
10 years ago in 2016, we were on version 1.9, the combat update. Think about how much the game has evolved since then. (If you really want to think, the entirety of Minecraft to that point had been built in just 7 years) The game will be very different again in 2036 - or at least, you'd really hope so. So what are the big things you think it should include?
As an example, here are my suggestions - they're deliberately high-level and don't go into every detail, that's the point. They're also still in the theme of vanilla minecraft - ie they're not incongruously modern or inappropriately horrific.

- more options around sharing the game, including the the ability to add mods to realms, or to share worlds between family members without having to have a second device
- new game modes that provide more options for players to choose what kind of game they want to play, including a hybrid creative/survival mode, an ultra-realistic survival mode, and creating workarounds for the problems with peaceful mode

- more biomes, passive, mobs, structures and NPCs in the Nether and (especially) the End, and much more functional (rather than just visual) variety between biomes in the Overworld
-better NPC AI, and more ways to interact and cooperate with villagers, pillagers and traders other than just buying stuff or killing them

- the ability to upgrade workbenches in order to unlock new recipes as you progress through the game. For example, a larger crafting table or brewing stand, and new workbenches that provide new crafting mechanics for the end game. Perhaps some of these workbenches aren't themselves craftable, but only exist in rare structures that you have to seek out to use.
- An expansion of the building process to include building either mobile or instantly breakable structures. So this would allow for people to construct their own tents, boats, wagons, ghast baskets. My idea is that this would require a redstone-enabled assembly platform.

The key point: all these ideas would interact so you get NPCs with their upgraded AI going around on the new mobile structures, and the difference between upgraded biomes is particularly noticeable in ultra-realistic mode. etc etc
Anyway - so what are your BIG ideas for Minecraft 36.1?

text:
The Inventory Problem™️

Since this is a hot topic among the community and keeps coming up in discussion regarding new updates, I wanted to drop in my two cents since these points usually get buried under piles of complaints and plain counterpoints that complaints are entitled.
# The core issue

The raw number of different items and blocks has expanded significantly and will keep doing so, no way around it. While back in the day, an inventory of 36 slots was enough to carry just about everything you'd ever need realistically, this has changed.
Undeniably, the amount of items multiplied immensely since these days, build styles have emerged that were not a thing back then, build palettes have become more complex. Mobs drop more stuff, not on a per-mob basis but the overall variety of drops. Environments have more ambient plants and various doodads. Redstone requires more and more specialized components.

Of course this is a good thing. It's a natural consequence of the game being alive and well.
It does mean however that things that used to be quick and easy to do have become more cumbersome. And solving this will always have to be compatible with both Java and Bedrock, all supported deviced and all the supported input methods from touch through gamepad to mouse/keyboard and beyond.
# The suggested change

> Just increase the inventory, that'd fix everything

Lots of people usually request this not seeing that, no, it wouldn't fix everything. And Mojang know this.

Increasing the inventory has a couple of issues that people like to overlook. It's fighting inflating numbers with inflating other numbers.
We already established that the raw number of items in this game will continue to grow. This is inevitable. This means if increasing the inventory is the fix, the player's inventory will become unwieldy. People will complain that they can't find in their inventories what they need to access. Depending on the client they might need to scroll. The next request will be tabbed inventory, a bigger hotbar, more hotbars, bigger stack sizes, ...
Players will have to juggle more and more types of tools, weapons, blocks, decoration, redstone components, whatever depending on what they're doing at the moment. Controlling a cursor with a gamepad across a huge grid of items could become troublesome, especially if it has to happen quickly.
# Mojang's approach

Mojang is already tackling this problem in very smart ways and people often dismiss these approaches, thinking each one of them is supposed to solve "the" inventory problem while each solves "a" inventory issue and collectively they will solve it sustainably.

A quick recap on what we have right now:

  * 2013: Donkeys and Mules have the ability to carry chests, effectively increasing the player's inventory on land by 15 slots.
  * 2016: Shulker Boxes allow the player to carry chests with their whole inventory, 27 additional slots in a single slot. Llamas also offer the ability to carry chests, but in contrast to donkeys and mules, they have the caravan mechanic which means up to nine llamas in sum can increase a player's inventory on land by 135 slots.
  * 2019: The barrel is a slightly cheaper storage option, the stonecutter reduces the number of items you usually need to transport while building. Campfires allow cooking food without using the inventory.

  * 2022: Chest Boats are added, increasing the inventory on water by 27 slots. Allays offer a new option for handling items in specific situations without needing to spend time in the inventory. While this was a community vote, the choice to offer the allay was very much concious on Mojang's side.
  * 2023: The decorated pot and the chiseled bookshelf also reduce the amount the player actually spends in their inventory when using certain items.

  * 2024: The crafter again reduces the amount the player actually is required to handle stuff in their inventory manually. Bundles allow stacking multiple, up to 64, different items in a single slot.
  * 2025: Leads allow transport of multiple chest mobs and chest boats at the same time, immensely increasing the player's effective inventory. Copper Golems were conciously picked up from a past vote by Mojang, and explicitly changed from their former mechanic to a new behaviour which, again, offers to reduce the time a player is required to spend in their inventory.
Shelves allow swapping up to 9 inventory slots at once without even opening the inventory, streamlining the handling of items and tools immensely.
# Observations

Especially in the more recent years, it's incredibly obvious that Mojang know perfectly well that inventory and item handling are a very complex problem that need a series of parallel approaches to solve them reliably for good.

They apparently try to follow multiple philosophies at the same time:

  * In general reduce the time the player needs to spend in the inventory at all

  * Make handling items in specific situations more streamlined
  * Increase the inventory in specific situations with trade-offs
And this is a way smarter approach than just increasing the inventory flat out. If done well, reducing the time in the inventory means players are less likely to run into situations where the inventory becomes a problem at all. Streamlining handling items means situations where the inventory has become a problem are quicker and easier to deal with.
Increasing the inventory with trade-offs then allows for niche situations to offer a bonus while asking the player to actually engage with the game's mechanics.
# The future

From these observations we can make a few fair estimations as to where we're headed.

  * Increased inventory while travelling across lava. I think Striders carrying chests is too obvious, but some kind of other lavaborne, swimming mob that can carry a few chests while being slower than the Strider seems likely to me.
  * A more streamlined way to specifically handle only tools and weapons inside the inventory. Some kind of toolbelt that allows to stack multiple tools into one slot and allows switching between them without needing to open the inventory.

  * Switching of the currently equipped armor quickly. This might be done as an update to the armor stand or as a new block that works like the powered shelf and allows for switching the currently equipped whole armor set with the stored one.
  * A palette item storing a variety of dyes for using multiple dyes without handling them in the inventory manually.
  * More direct interactions with blocks for specialized storage. I could see specialized record racks for storing stacks of record discs, some kind of pantry for holding food items, storing an arbitrary amount of one color dye in a paint bucket block, potion racks, specialized storage for ores, ingots, seeds, among others. These will most likely be handling a single type of item with huge variations or a lot of different items that all work the same way.
  * A way to simply replace a block or transform it in its location. Examples would be a smelting spell that transforms a block into its furnace output at a cost or cuts blank stone into bricks or logs into planks. Maybe something that allows the transformation of any already placed wood product into a different wood.
In my opinion, we are actually likely to see a couple of these across the next couple of years. If a simple increased inventory comes at all, it will probably come at a cost. A backpack that gives a single extra row of 9 slots at the cost of not being able to wear armor is a common suggestion that seems realistic to me. But I don't think this will actually be that necessary long term, if the already established philosophies are followed and implemented to their full potential.
Solving the situations where the inventory frustration actually comes up is way more useful than delaying the problem a couple updates into the future.

Minecraft desperately needs more enchantments: not stronger ones, just more interesting ones

Anyone else feel like enchanting in Minecraft has basically been solved for years?

Every survival world ends with the exact same gear:

Mending Unbreaking III Prot IV Efficiency V Sharpness V

The problem is not balance. The problem is lack of choice.
Minecraft is at its best when players solve problems differently, but enchantments barely allow different playstyles anymore. Everyone just builds the objectively correct setup.

I do not want power creep. I want weird, niche, fun enchantments that actually change gameplay.

Stuff like:

  * vein mining with durability tradeoff

  * shield enchants

  * movement based boot enchants

  * xbow/bow enchants focused on utility instead of damage

  * Elytra enchants with pros and cons
  * weapon enchants that reward timing/combat style

Also, enchant progression basically ends after villagers. Once you get a trading hall, you skip almost all loot progression forever.

Ancient Cities, Trial Chambers, End structures, mineshafts, dungeons, ocean monuments, all of them could have unique enchantments or upgrade paths worth exploring for - or even give us enchants we can only obtain using rare(r) items/blocks collected in more end game environments.
Right now enchanting feels less like building a character and more like filling out a checklist once per world. It desperately needs some thought and love.
